content: Malaria is the most frequent trigger for crises in individuals with sickle cell disease living in regions where malaria is endemic. In these areas, healthcare professionals often recommend lifelong malaria chemoprophylaxis for people with sickle cell disease. Therefore, it is crucial to have robust evidence supporting the benefits of this intervention. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of routine malaria chemoprophylaxis in individuals with sickle cell disease. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies up to January 2006. Additionally, reference lists were reviewed, and relevant organizations and pharmaceutical companies were contacted. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the use of any antimalarial drug for at least three months with either a placebo or no intervention. Two independent authors applied these criteria, assessed the risk of bias in the studies, and extracted data. Dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Two trials, involving a total of 223 children with homozygous sickle cell disease, met the inclusion criteria. The first trial, a randomized controlled study conducted in Nigeria, compared two different antimalarial drugs with a placebo. This trial demonstrated that malaria chemoprophylaxis significantly reduced the frequency of sickle cell crises (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.83; 97 children), hospital admissions (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.63; 97 participants), and the need for blood transfusions (RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.56; 97 participants). The second trial, a quasi-randomized controlled study conducted in Uganda, involved 126 children. This trial compared the use of an antimalarial drug combined with antibiotics to no antimalarial treatment plus a placebo. The results showed that chemoprophylaxis reduced the number of malaria episodes and dactylitis occurrences. Additionally, it was associated with an increase in mean hemoglobin levels. In conclusion, the evidence supports the routine use of malaria chemoprophylaxis in individuals with sickle cell disease living in malaria-endemic regions. This intervention has been shown to reduce the frequency of sickle cell crises, hospitalizations, and blood transfusions, while also improving hemoglobin levels and reducing malaria-related complications.
